evaluation.positioning_hook: A burned-out orbital depot crew discovers their station is being quietly compressed, reclassified as assets, and prepared for harvest — and the only way out may be to crash the system before it crashes them.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, sellable engine: a workplace sci-fi nightmare that turns into survival horror with a corporate conspiracy spine. The audience is real and genre-literate, though the bleakness and abstract escalation narrow it more toward adult genre buyers than four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: a space depot crew notices reality bending, then learns the station is literally shrinking and their lives are being valued as insurance assets. The insurance matrix, the orbital decay reveal, and the final preservation-room turn make the premise easy to pitch in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Miller, Sarah, Vance, and Riggs each have distinct behavioral signatures, and the script gives them playable friction through work banter, distrust, and crisis response. Miller is the clearest anchor, but the ensemble is more functional than deeply revelatory, with most characters defined by role and attitude rather than layered contradiction.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s strongest move is making corporate dehumanization literal through insurance valuation, asset language, and a preservation-room coda that reframes the whole story as processing. The compression motif, the Sim-Gate reality bleed, and the final monochrome archive sequence give it a confident, ownable sci-fi voice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script escalates cleanly from anomaly to body horror to structural collapse to escape, with each reveal changing the crew’s objective. The lion attack, the asset matrix, the orbital decay discovery, and the decompression breach all function as strong propulsion beats.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a station being treated as a living accounting problem is fresh and immediately legible, especially once the crew realizes the system is learning them as assets. The ending’s preservation-room reveal makes the premise feel both surprising and inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The depot feels lived-in and operational: coffee, shift fatigue, maintenance trusses, legacy systems, PPE, insurance matrices, and corporate protocol all create a coherent industrial ecosystem. The world generates story because every tool, system, and hierarchy can turn hostile.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct tonal blend of deadpan workplace banter, creeping cosmic dread, and body-horror inevitability. The contrast between chip jokes, corporate jargon, and catastrophic decompression gives it a hard-to-mistake register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The preservation-room coda and the repeated language of assets, processing, and transfer suggest a larger system beyond the depot. The script hints at a broader machine, but most of the depth is implied rather than dramatized through secondary relationships or a wider institutional map.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The crew banter gives the script a usable ensemble rhythm, especially Miller/Sarah/Vance/Dixon, and the workplace dynamic creates recurring friction. Still, the relationships are strongest as crisis-response chemistry rather than a truly generative ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Miller McCord
lead_characters.hook: The crew’s quiet center of gravity: observant, exhausted, and harder to read than he wants anyone to know. Miller carries himself like a man who has already accepted too much, but once he realizes the depot is classifying people as inventory, his restraint turns into command.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Michael B. Jordan in a contained pressure-cooker role or a John Boyega-style performance: controlled authority under strain, then a late-breaking moral pivot that lets the actor play intelligence, hurt, and action in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Sarah Beaumont
lead_characters.hook: The emotional truth-teller in the room, with the kind of dry, unforced confidence that makes her the first person to say what everyone else is thinking. Sarah is practical, funny, and sharper than the men around her give her credit for, which makes her one of the script’s most immediately watchable presences.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same appeal as Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers: grounded wit, moral clarity, and a pressure-cooker scene partner who can hold the room without overplaying it.

lead_characters.name: Vance Matheson
lead_characters.hook: Fast-talking, brainy, and perpetually one caffeine crash away from panic, Vance is the script’s best conduit for technical exposition without losing personality. He reads like the guy who jokes to stay ahead of fear, then surprises you by becoming the one who can actually solve the problem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong territory for a Paul Dano or Jesse Plemons type of performance: nervous intelligence, comic timing, and the chance to turn a talky support role into a memorable survival pivot.

lead_characters.name: Riggs
lead_characters.hook: The depot manager who treats human beings like line items and never drops the corporate mask until the mask becomes the horror. Riggs is funny in a mean, bureaucratic way, then increasingly unsettling as the script reveals how much of the system he has internalized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Bryan Cranston did in Breaking Bad’s early corporate-adjacent menace or what Matthew Macfadyen does with polished cruelty: authority, denial, and a slow collapse into something uglier.

lead_characters.name: Dixon
lead_characters.hook: The loudest guy in the room, but not the least intelligent; Dixon is the pressure valve, the skeptic, and the one most likely to say the thing everyone else is thinking with a laugh. He gives the script its roughest comic texture and some of its most human panic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great character-actor part in the vein of Walton Goggins in a pressure-cooker ensemble: swagger, irritation, and the chance to turn comic defiance into real pathos.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Patricia Aris
lead_characters.hook: Dry, self-possessed, and quietly formidable, Dr. Aris is the one person who can speak corporate, medical, and survival language without blinking. Her calm is not softness; it’s competence sharpened into resistance, and the script smartly lets her become the person who knows how to leave.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige-supporting territory in the mold of Annette Bening in 20th Century Women or Rebecca Ferguson in Dune: intelligence, authority, and a late-script reveal of hidden agency.

lead_characters.name: Hendrix
lead_characters.hook: A physically imposing technician with a dry sense of humor and a body that already feels out of place in the depot’s geometry. Hendrix is one of the script’s best visual ideas: a giant who reads the room faster than the room can contain him, making his fate hit hard.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a rare showcase for a performer with unusual physical presence, similar to what Dave Bautista gets when the role lets size, vulnerability, and deadpan humor coexist.

lead_characters.name: Henderson
lead_characters.hook: The polished corporate voice on the other end of the line, all privilege and plausible deniability. Henderson is less a person than a system avatar, which makes him useful as a pressure source and a symbol of the hierarchy above the depot.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sleek, contemptuous supporting role that lets an actor do controlled menace in the style of Nicholas Hoult or Tom Hiddleston when they’re playing polished institutional power.

lead_characters.name: Robert
lead_characters.hook: A working-body presence in the crew, useful for grounding the depot as a real workplace rather than a concept. Robert is less defined than the other principals, but he helps sell the station’s lived-in labor texture and becomes part of the ensemble’s panic response.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid ensemble utility work for a character actor who can make procedural labor feel specific, the kind of part that benefits from naturalism and timing more than speeches.

lead_characters.name: Engineer #2
lead_characters.hook: A functional crew member whose death is the script’s first hard proof that the anomaly is lethal. He’s not written as a full character, but his role is structurally important because the lion attack turns the premise from weird to fatal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a brief but high-impact genre role: the kind of early casualty that gives an actor a memorable exit and the script a clean escalation point.

lead_characters.name: Technician
lead_characters.hook: The final image of the script, a monochrome administrator who resembles Riggs just enough to make the whole story feel processed rather than resolved. He is calm, detached, and chillingly procedural, which makes the ending land as a bureaucratic afterlife rather than a victory.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is eerie, minimalist showcase material in the vein of a late-film reveal performance like Ralph Fiennes in The Grand Budapest Hotel’s colder registers or a Michael Shannon-style deadpan authority turn.

casting_characteristics: Hendrix requires a very tall performer or a strong visual effects/forced-perspective solution
Miller is a Black male lead in his 40s
Ensemble skews adult, working-age, with no child roles

notable_requirements: Primary build is an orbital depot interior with connected corridors, control rooms, medical bay, and maintenance truss
Exterior EVA and lifepod platform work require space-facing visual effects and controlled stunt safety

technical.vfx_details: Space exteriors, orbital depot vistas, Sim-Gate environment prints, reality distortion effects, decompression event, station collapse, and the final preservation-room visual language all require compositing and digital enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, decompression effects, environmental lighting shifts, suit compression gag, and body-impact beats for the lion attack and station failure.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original, specialty theatrical, or premium-genre label with adult sci-fi/horror positioning

budget.note: The depot build, space exteriors, Sim-Gate effects, and collapse sequence push this above a simple contained thriller, but it still lives in a scopeable genre range if the station is designed as a reusable primary set.

casting.note: Miller needs a lead who can carry quiet authority and escalating dread, and Hendrix’s 7'2" physical requirement narrows the pool. The ensemble is otherwise castable with strong character actors.

development.note: The concept is clear, but the final preservation-room reveal and the abstract system logic will need careful framing so the ending reads as a payoff rather than a left turn. The script’s commercial identity is strongest when the workplace horror and corporate conspiracy stay foregrounded.

comp_set.title: Life
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the contained-space escalation and the sense of a crew trapped with an intelligent, lethal anomaly in a high-pressure environment.

comp_set.title: Pandorum
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the claustrophobic sci-fi survival lane, with a damaged vessel, institutional secrecy, and a creeping realization that the environment itself is the threat.

comp_set.title: Aniara
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on existential space dread and the slow realization that the crew’s situation is not recoverable, only endured.

comp_set.title: The Platform
comp_set.why_it_comps: The corporate/class allegory and the brutal logic of people being sorted by system rules give it a similar social-horror edge.

comp_set.title: Moon
comp_set.why_it_comps: The isolated industrial sci-fi setting, corporate exploitation, and identity-as-asset reveal place it in the same adult genre conversation.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult genre audiences who like smart, claustrophobic sci-fi with horror escalation and corporate satire.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily 25-54, skewing male but with strong crossover for women who respond to elevated survival thrillers and ensemble workplace dynamics.

budget_tier.note: A reusable orbital-depot build, moderate VFX, and a handful of exterior space/EVA sequences keep this in mid-budget feature territory rather than full studio scale.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult genre lane where concept clarity, contained geography, and a strong lead performance can outweigh the absence of franchise IP. The corporate-horror angle and the final preservation-room reveal give it a sharper identity than a standard space survival piece.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The ending suggests a larger system, but no supporting character or world vector is developed enough to justify a sequel or spinoff package.

strengths.what_it_means: The script turns workplace dehumanization into a clean commercial engine, which is exactly the kind of hook that helps a buyer understand the movie in one sentence. That makes it attractive to genre execs looking for elevated sci-fi with a social edge and to actors who want a role with moral weight, not just survival mechanics.
strengths.evidence: The crew discovers the insurance matrix classifying them as assets, with Miller valued at 4.2 million and Engineer #2 already in claim processing.

strengths.what_it_means: The depot gives the film a producible spine: one primary build can carry most of the story while the escalation feels bigger than the footprint. That is the sweet spot for buyers who want a premium-looking genre piece without tentpole spend.
strengths.evidence: Most of the script plays in commons, control rooms, corridors, the Sim-Gate, and the lifepod platform, with space exteriors used strategically.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A lead role built for restraint
strengths.what_it_means: Miller is the kind of part that can elevate a mid-career actor or reframe a rising one, because the performance lives in control, observation, and delayed eruption. That is valuable to buyers because it creates attachment leverage without requiring a star to carry every scene on volume.
strengths.evidence: Miller clocks the anomalies before others do, withholds the insurance reveal until he can prove it, and becomes the crew’s center as the station collapses.

strengths.what_it_means: The monochrome preservation-room coda gives the script a sticky ending that recontextualizes the whole story as processing rather than escape. That kind of button helps marketing, trailer construction, and post-screening conversation because it leaves the audience with a clean, unsettling image.
strengths.evidence: The Technician’s archive room, the asset drawer labels, and the final line about it being their turn.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has enough character chemistry to keep the middle from becoming pure mechanics, which broadens its appeal beyond hard sci-fi fans. Buyers looking for a castable ensemble piece will see room for recognizable actors to make the material pop.
strengths.evidence: Sarah’s dry one-liners, Dixon’s profanity-laced skepticism, and Vance’s nervous technical humor keep the depot feeling inhabited.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, producible adult sci-fi thriller with a sharp corporate-horror premise and a contained industrial setting that can deliver premium scale without tentpole spend. The combination of a strong lead role, ensemble banter, and a final-image twist gives it real streamer and specialty-genre appeal.

items.area: The ending shifts into abstraction fast.
items.detail: The preservation-room reveal is striking, but it pivots from survival thriller into a more conceptual processing-space coda in the last pages. That is a real buyer conversation because the final movement changes the movie’s promise from escape drama to metaphysical inventory.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid, but not equally deep.
items.detail: Miller, Sarah, Vance, and Riggs all have clear functions, but only Miller is built with enough contradiction to feel fully lead-level. A producer will see a strong cast package, but also notice that several supporting roles are more sharply drawn as types than as fully dimensional engines.

items.area: The VFX burden is concentrated in key sequences.
items.detail: The Sim-Gate distortions, the shrinking geometry, the decompression breach, and the station collapse all need to land cleanly for the concept to pay off. That keeps the movie in mid-budget territory, but it also means the effects plan has to be disciplined rather than decorative.

The 7'2" physical requirement is a real casting constraint, and the role also needs comic timing and technical credibility. That combination makes the part memorable, but it is not a casual open-call role.

items.area: The corporate logic is intentionally opaque.
items.detail: The insurance matrix, asset language, and preservation system are compelling, but the script keeps the larger machine just abstract enough that some buyers will want a clearer sense of the governing rules. That is not a clearance issue; it is a development conversation about how much mystery the market will tolerate before the third-act payoff.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest commercial risk is that its final act leans into conceptual processing-room imagery after spending most of its runtime as a grounded survival thriller. The other friction points are manageable but real: a mid-budget VFX plan, a narrow Hendrix casting lane, and an ensemble that is strong in function but not uniformly deep.
